summary: Coney Island Light on Norton's Point, first lit 1 August 1890; automated 1989; Coast Guard property inside the gated Sea Gate community; landmark hearing pending.

lens.where: Coast Guard Headquarters, Washington, D.C. (removed 1989, LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: 61 ft (18.6 m) from base to lantern (archive). Archive gives 1920 as the year the present tower was established; see resolved_conflicts.

structures.type: square wooden tower on four concrete footings
structures.note: Removed to the depot and site sold at auction (1896).
Archive gives the quarters year as 1896; LighthouseFriends says work on the dwelling began in 1890.

access.note: Inside the gates of Sea Gate, a private community closed to non-residents. The archive lists the station as not open to the public.

visit.note: Tours have become rare since Frank Schubert's death in 2003 (Gothamist).

facts.ownership: Coast Guard owns the lighthouse and leases it to the Sea Gate Association (Hoodline, citing 6sqft).

events.note: Congress statute for a Norton's Point light; $25,000 for two range lights (2 March 1889 per Coney Island History Project).
Owners asked twice the land's estimated value; the site was condemned and acquired for $3,500.
Rear skeletal steel tower erected; Gothamist and Hoodline describe a tower built in 1890.
Fourth-order light established 1 August 1890; lit by Keeper Thomas Higginbotham.
Original fourth-order Fresnel lens, kerosene, red flash.
Fog bell moved to a new position; close board fence built along two sides of the reservation.
Front beacon removed to the general lighthouse depot; site sold at public auction (6 July 1896 per LighthouseFriends).
From a red flash every ten seconds to a red flash every five seconds (30 June 1899).
House about 250 yards east of the light washed away; 600-foot stone wall built in 1915, undermined by a storm within six months.
Storm of 10 to 12 April 1918: north corner of the reservation cut away; fog-signal house fell into the water; apparatus recovered.
Archive: present tower established 1920 (conflicts with 1890; see resolved_conflicts).
Adrien J. Boisvert transferred from Fire Island Lighthouse to replace Herbert L. Greenwood.
Frank P. Schubert becomes keeper; kept the light until his death in 2003.
Original fourth-order lens removed and sent to Coast Guard Headquarters, Washington, D.C.
Landmarks Preservation Commission votes (20 October 2026) to schedule a public hearing on the tower and keeper's dwelling for landmark designation.

corrections.why: The archive gives 75 ft (22.9 m) as the height of the light above water and 61 ft (18.6 m) as the tower's height from base to lantern. The 23.0 m in the record matches the focal height.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Board's report for fiscal 1891 and 1892 shows the Norton's Point light established on 1 August 1890, so 1890 is the first lighting. The archive's 1920 date for the present tower is not explained by these sources and is left open.

notes_for_editor: 1) Tower date: the archive (USLHS) gives 1920 as the year the present tower was established and the archive's place record gives 1920 for the tower; Gothamist and Hoodline say 1890; LighthouseFriends says the original rear tower remains standing. I found no primary report that settles it; the Commissioner and Bulletin texts for 1918-1922 that the corpus search returned do not mention a new tower. Check the NYC Landmarks calendaring report (nyc.gov, calendaring dated 20 Oct 2026); fetch_text returned 403 for it and it was not read. 2) Higginbotham's July 1910 death is from LighthouseFriends only. A Chronicling America search of NY papers for July to September 1910 did not find it (the Higginbotham hits were other men). 3) Keeper's dwelling date: archive gives 1896, LighthouseFriends says work began 1890. 4) Height: the record's structures height 23.0 m equals the focal height; the tower is 61 ft (18.6 m) base to lantern per the archive. 5) Fog bell and fence (FY1891) is from OCR text; the snippet reads 'Coneg Island' in OCR; quotes are as OCR'd. 6) Privacy: Frank Schubert's connection ended 2003; the story names him only in his public role and does not repeat family details beyond what Gothamist prints. Boisvert's family details are omitted. The grandson-run family website is not named. 7) LighthouseFriends and Hoodline and Gothamist are copyrighted; the story paraphrases them and uses at most one short quotation of a sentence (LighthouseFriends 'remains standing'). 8) The USCG Historian page (history.uscg.mil) returned 403 through the archive copy; its facts are used only as Hoodline reports them. 9) The Life-Saving Service's Coney Island station (No. 37, Third District) is a separate station and is not part of this story. 10) Schubert's 'last civilian keeper' claim is a Gothamist and LighthouseFriends claim ('believed'), not verified. 11) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Commissioner's 1921 note (scan p.688, printed p.83) says the reservation 'was purchased in 1889'; LighthouseFriends and Hoodline say the owners' asking price led to condemnation for $3,500. The story states this disagreement; the sources do not explain it. 12) The archive's keeper's-quarters year (1896) and construction (wood) differ from LighthouseFriends (work began 1890) and Hoodline (brick cottage). Stated in the story. 13) The fog-bell entry (scan p.79 of the 1891-92 volume, OCR 'Coneg Island') falls in the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891, so 'fiscal year 1891' holds. 14) LighthouseFriends says Greenwood was in charge for twenty-three years; the archive's 1919-1941 span gives about twenty-two. The story attributes the figure to LighthouseFriends.
